A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AstaBench study and contain readable main text and Appendices A–H. Tables, figures, equations, and relocated material support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 57 agents across 22 architectural classes, including benchmark scores and computational costs in Tables 4–17.

after.justification: v2 retains these original evaluations and adds human-judgment comparisons, rubric-bias experiments, and quantified grading-validation results.

M1.justification: The Asta Environment, agent architectures, routing procedures, and core scoring approaches are retained. The ReAct step limit and expanded description of three-facet grading disclose implementation details without establishing a procedural change.

E1.justification: The same 11 benchmarks and task coverage remain. CORE-Bench-Hard is renamed CORE-Bench-Hard−, but GPU-requiring instances were already excluded in v1, Appendix E.6. New domain distributions describe existing datasets, and validation studies use retained benchmark questions.

E2.justification: The new human-ranking comparison in Appendix E.3 includes a fine-tuned Qwen3-8B model alongside five previously evaluated agents. Main benchmark comparators remain unchanged; the GPT-5-mini row added to Table 8 redisplays results already present in v1 Table 15.

E3.justification: Appendix E.3 adds three-answer expert comparisons across the 100 test questions, sampling from six systems, and controlled rubric-construction experiments with held-out systems and different contributor counts. These extend validation protocols within existing benchmarks; the original splits, corpus cutoffs, and primary evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: v1 primarily supported ScholarQA-CS2 judging through agreement between two Gemini judges and described end-to-end grading spot-checks without quantified outcomes. v2 adds expert-ranking validation, rubric-source bias and contributor-count sensitivity analyses, and detailed analysis of grading decisions across reports, code, and artifacts. These substantially expand tests of benchmark validity.

E5.justification: Table 11 and Figure 2 add aggregate uncertainty reporting. Appendix D newly documents 95% confidence intervals, sample-based standard errors, and weighted propagation under task independence. Appendix E.3 also introduces significance reporting for rubric holdout experiments. Per-benchmark confidence intervals already existed; increased repeated runs or seed counts are not reported.

E6.justification: Primary benchmark means are retained, but substantial validation results are added: system-level human agreement of Kendall tau 0.467, 68.1% agreement on clear-winner instances, rubric holdout drops averaging 2.5 points for three systems, and 92% grading correctness on 50 development rubric items. Table 20 adds complete-task success rates of 0–5%; dataset distributions and displayed efficiency frontiers also change. The new 37% GPT-5-mini statement in Section 5 conflicts with 34.6% in Tables 8 and 15.

T1.justification: Existing task and scoring definitions are retained, with no added theorem, proof, or substantive theoretical revision. The new standard-error propagation formula documents statistical estimation rather than changing the underlying mathematical framework.

C1.justification: The abstract and Introduction remove priority claims that AstaBench is the first holistic scientific-research benchmark, although Section 3 retains similar wording. Claims about standardized tools, broad agent evaluation, and scientific research assistance remaining unsolved are preserved.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands qualifications about evaluation validity: citation metrics do not verify source or quotation authenticity, rubric construction can favor contributing systems, and human agreement is imperfect. It interprets additional rubric contributors as mitigating bias and details end-to-end grading failures involving vague evidence or incorrect implementation nuances. These materially extend v1's limited caveats.

D1.justification: New disclosures include ReAct's 100-step cap, removal of quoted snippets from systems lacking literature access, and the consistency rule combining report, code, and artifact judgments. The grading spot-check's sample size and statistical calculations are also documented more precisely. These additions do not establish changes to the original implementation or execution budgets.

R1.justification: v2 adds Kapoor et al. (2024), AI Agents That Matter, to support cost-aware evaluation in the Introduction and Appendix A. It also modestly narrows novelty language; the substantive related-work survey otherwise remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The revision reorders the introductory list of benchmarking deficiencies, adds targeted validation and statistical explanations, clarifies benchmark terminology and cross-references, and introduces the ICLR 2026 publication header. The overall section structure and extensive task examples and prompts are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 18–21 and Figure 10, reformats Table 11, adds aggregate error bars to Figure 2, and redraws frontier displays and legends. Several existing tables and figures are compacted or relocated; v1 Tables 18–19 become Tables 22–23. These are localized additions and display revisions rather than a wholesale redesign.

improvement.justification: Expert validation and rubric-bias tests in Appendix E.3, quantified grading checks in F.9, and aggregate uncertainty reporting make the benchmark's reliability more assessable than in v1. These targeted gains improve transparency without resolving the documented grading and rubric biases. A new 37% versus 34.6% prose/table inconsistency slightly offsets the gains, yielding a limited overall improvement.
